# Albinder Dhindsa: Zomato Bought His Struggling Startup. Now He Runs Zomato's Parent.
URL: https://boardroomcxo.com/article-albinder-dhindsa-blinkit
Published: 2026-10-31
Author: CA Ketul Patel, Founder, Boardroom CXO
Publisher: Boardroom CXO (https://boardroomcxo.com)
================================================================================

## Key Takeaways

- Grofers renamed itself Blinkit in December 2021 to bet on 10-minute grocery delivery. By March 2022 it had laid off staff in several cities and Zomato had approved a loan of up to $150 million. In June 2022 Zomato agreed to buy it in an all-stock deal.
- In July to September 2022, Blinkit lost ₹259 crore at the adjusted EBITDA level on orders worth ₹1,482 crore, and Zomato told shareholders that most investors gave it zero value. Co-founder Albinder Dhindsa stayed to run it: "Growth is the biggest lever driving improvement in profitability."
- Blinkit's net order value overtook Zomato's food delivery in April to June 2025. A year later, with 2,443 dark stores, it made ₹102 crore of adjusted EBITDA in a quarter, and Dhindsa became CEO of Eternal. Boards should think hard before letting the founder of an acquired business walk away.

> "I know that most investors currently ascribe zero value to the Blinkit business, and that's understandable."

Deepinder Goyal, then CEO of Zomato, wrote that in the company's shareholder letter in November 2022.

Zero.

## How Blinkit Got There

To see why, go back a year. In December 2021, Grofers renamed itself Blinkit and bet the business on one promise: groceries in about 10 minutes.

The bet burned cash fast. By March 2022, Blinkit had let go of staff across several cities, closed some dark stores and delayed some vendor payments. Zomato approved a loan of up to $150 million to keep it going.

In June 2022, Zomato agreed to buy Blinkit in an all-stock deal. The losses continued. In the July to September 2022 quarter, Blinkit lost ₹259 crore at the adjusted EBITDA level, on orders worth about ₹1,482 crore.

## Who Is Albinder Dhindsa?

Albinder Dhindsa is the co-founder of Blinkit and, since February 2026, chief executive of Eternal, the listed company that owns Zomato and Blinkit.

An IIT Delhi graduate with an MBA from Columbia, he spent three years at Zomato, latterly as head of international operations, before leaving in 2014 to build Grofers.

## He Stayed

When Zomato bought Blinkit, he stayed on to run it.

Most founders would have taken the exit and moved on. A sale at a low valuation, after layoffs and a rescue loan, is the natural moment to leave.

He did not. He stayed with the 10-minute idea and focused on making it pay. In the same November 2022 letter, he set out how:

> "Growth is the biggest lever driving improvement in profitability. Higher throughput leads to growth in revenue per order as well as lower cost, given the high operating leverage in this business."

So he scaled. More dark stores, closer to homes, in more cities. More categories beyond groceries.

## What Staying Delivered

The turn came in numbers. In the April to June 2025 quarter, Blinkit's net order value, ₹9,203 crore, overtook Zomato's own food delivery business for the first time.

A year later, in April to June 2026, Blinkit ran 2,443 dark stores. The business that had lost ₹259 crore in a quarter made ₹102 crore of adjusted EBITDA in one.

One more twist. In 2014, Dhindsa left a job at Zomato to build Grofers. On 1 February 2026, he became CEO of Eternal, the company that now owns Zomato, when Deepinder Goyal stepped back from the role.

## The Boardroom Lesson: The Market Cannot Price Who Stays

When a business is sold cheaply, its valuation tells you what investors think of its past. It says little about the person running it, and whether they will stay long enough to change the answer.

> The market can price a business at zero. It cannot price the person who refuses to leave it.

Zomato's decision to keep the founder in charge, and Dhindsa's decision to stay, turned a written-off acquisition into the largest part of the group.

## Common Mistakes Boards Make After Acquiring a Founder-Led Business

Boards that buy a struggling founder-led company tend to make the same three errors.

They let the founder leave with the cheque. The founder often understands the model's economics better than anyone. Losing them at the low point can mean losing the turnaround.

They replace the bet with the parent's playbook. Zomato did not turn Blinkit into a slower, safer grocery business. It let the 10-minute model scale.

They judge the deal on the first year's losses. Blinkit's numbers in 2022 looked like a mistake. The fair test was what the business did once it reached scale.

## A Framework for Keeping Founders After an Acquisition

When we brief boards on a leadership search linked to an acquisition, we push for three specific checks.
- Ask whether the founder still believes in the model. A founder who stays out of conviction is worth more than one held by an earn-out.
- Agree what success looks like, in numbers. Dhindsa's case rested on throughput and operating leverage. Boards should know which metrics will show whether the bet is working.
- Plan for the founder's next role. The person who turns around an acquired business may be the group's next leader. Build that into succession planning early.

## Why This Belongs in the Boardroom, Not Just the Business Pages

This sits alongside the story we told of Saugata Gupta at Marico, who bought founder-led brands and kept the parent company out of their way. Zomato did the same with Blinkit, and the founder ended up running the whole group.

A valuation is a verdict on the past. The person who stays writes the next one.

## Sources

- Business Today, Grofers rebrands to Blinkit in line with its 10-min grocery delivery plan, December 2021
- Inc42, Zomato to give $150 Mn loan to Blinkit, March 2022
- Zomato Limited (BSE filing), Shareholders' letter, Q2 FY23, November 2022
- MediaNama, Zomato Q1 FY26 earnings: Blinkit's net order value grows 127%, July 2025
- YourStory, Deepinder Goyal steps down as Eternal's Group CEO, January 2026
- YourStory, Coming full circle: Tracing the journey of Eternal's new CEO Albinder Dhindsa, January 2026
- Inc42, Blinkit's Q1 adjusted EBITDA rises to ₹102 Cr, July 2026

# Ajay Bijli's Sales Fell 92% in a Year. Now 150 Million People Buy His Tickets.
URL: https://boardroomcxo.com/article-ajay-bijli-pvr-inox
Published: 2026-10-30
Author: CA Ketul Patel, Founder, Boardroom CXO
Publisher: Boardroom CXO (https://boardroomcxo.com)
================================================================================

## Key Takeaways

- PVR began shutting its 845 screens across 71 cities on 11 March 2020. In FY21 its revenue from operations fell 92% to about ₹280 crore, and it lost about ₹748 crore.
- Ajay Bijli bet that audiences would come back and made survival the job: fixed costs cut 63%, rent down 79%, ₹1,600 crore of fresh equity and debt, popcorn sold online, and a merger with rival INOX completed in February 2023.
- In FY26 PVR INOX sold 150 million tickets across 1,798 screens and made a net profit of ₹333 crore, helped by a one-time gain from selling its popcorn business. Its average ticket price, ₹280, matched PVR's entire FY21 revenue in crore. Boards should judge a leader in a crisis on whether the business is still standing when demand returns.

In March 2020, India's cinemas were among the first businesses ordered to shut. PVR began closing its screens on 11 March. Within days, almost all of them were dark.

That was 845 screens across 71 cities, with nobody in the seats.

> "As a businessman, you can forecast volatility, but you can never forecast a zero-revenue situation," Ajay Bijli told YourStory in May 2020.

## What the Shutdown Cost

In FY21, PVR's revenue from operations fell 92%, to about ₹280 crore, from ₹3,414 crore the year before. It lost about ₹748 crore.

And the question hanging over the business was bigger than one bad year. Streaming was booming at home. Would people ever come back to the cinema?

## Who Is Ajay Bijli?

Ajay Bijli is the founder and managing director of PVR INOX. He built the business from one ageing cinema: his father's Priya Cinema in South Delhi, which he set about reviving in the early 1990s, refurbishing it, installing Dolby sound and showing Hollywood films.

In 1997, with Australia's Village Roadshow as partner, he opened PVR Anupam in Saket, India's first multiplex.

He had spent more than two decades building that business. In a few weeks, it had stopped earning.

## The Bet: Survive Until They Come Back

Bijli bet that audiences would return. So his job was to keep PVR alive until they did.

He cut PVR's fixed costs by 63% in FY21 compared with FY20. Rent alone fell 79%, with landlords agreeing to near-total waivers during the lockdown months. Common area charges fell 42%, and all other fixed overheads 57%.

He raised about ₹1,600 crore of fresh liquidity, ₹1,100 crore in equity and ₹500 crore in debt, to keep cash in the bank.

He even took PVR's popcorn out of the cinema. In August 2021, PopMagic, a microwave popcorn, went on sale on Amazon, after more than three lakh units were sold through cinemas and food delivery apps.

## The Merger With INOX

Once theatres reopened, he went further. In March 2022, PVR agreed to merge with its biggest rival, INOX Leisure. The merger was completed in February 2023, creating PVR INOX, with Bijli as managing director.

The logic was survival too. "The balance sheets of both companies got completely hammered in the pandemic and one of the ways to survive and make the companies strong was to merge," he told YourStory in May 2023.

> "The last three years have been life altering. We are fortunate to have survived this baptism by fire."

## What the Bet Delivered

The recovery was slow. PVR INOX lost money in FY25. But in FY26, it welcomed 150 million moviegoers across 1,798 screens in 113 cities and made a net profit of ₹333 crore, helped by a one-time gain of about ₹195 crore from selling its popcorn business, 4700BC.

One pair of numbers sums it up. In FY21, PVR's entire year of revenue was about ₹280 crore. In FY26, ₹280 was the price of an average PVR INOX ticket.

## The Boardroom Lesson: Conviction Needs a Survival Plan

In a crisis that takes revenue to almost nothing, conviction alone does not keep a company alive. Cash does. Bijli's belief that audiences would come back was only useful because he cut costs and raised capital fast enough to still be there when they did.

> A crisis can empty every seat. Conviction is what fills them again.

He paired the long-term bet with short-term discipline, and then used the downturn to make the company bigger, not smaller.

## Common Mistakes Boards Make in a Revenue Shock

Boards facing a sudden collapse in revenue tend to make the same three errors.

They wait to see how long it lasts. Every week of full fixed costs with no revenue burns cash. PVR's cost cuts and fund-raising came within months, not after the crisis had passed.

They treat the crisis as the end of the business model. Streaming looked like it would kill cinema. The leader's job is to judge whether demand is gone or only paused, and to bet accordingly.

They see a rival only as a competitor. The downturn that weakened PVR also weakened INOX. Merging made both stronger. Crises open doors that are closed in good times.

## A Framework for Hiring a Leader for a Crisis

When we brief boards on a CXO search for a business facing a sudden shock, we push for three specific checks.
- Ask how the candidate would protect cash in the first 90 days. The right leader can name the fixed costs to renegotiate and the capital to raise, and in what order.
- Test conviction against evidence. Ask candidates how they decided whether demand would return, and what would have changed their minds.
- Hire a CFO who can raise money in bad times. PVR raised ₹1,600 crore with its screens dark. A finance leader with investor and lender relationships is part of the survival plan.

## Why This Belongs in the Boardroom, Not Just the Business Pages

This sits alongside the story we told of Shailesh Chandra at Tata Motors, who took charge of a business at its lowest point a week after the country locked down. And PVR's popcorn brand, 4700BC, was bought by Marico, whose approach to buying young brands we wrote about in Saugata Gupta's story.

Every leader says they believe in the business. The crisis shows who planned to survive long enough to prove it.

## Sources

- Business Standard, PVR adds 4 more screens in Indore, March 2020
- YourStory, Why Ajay Bijli of PVR believes theatres will overcome the worst of times, including coronavirus, May 2020
- Business Standard, PVR Q4 net loss widens to Rs 289 cr, June 2021
- ICRA, PVR Limited rating rationale, February 2022
- afaqs, PVR PopMagic microwave popcorn launches on Amazon, August 2021
- YourStory, From 2019's historic highs to the pandemic's baptism by fire: How PVR Cinemas lived and learned, May 2023
- Free Press Journal, PVR INOX swings to Q4 profit of ₹186 crore, FY26 revenue rises 17%, May 2026
- Kotak Neo, PVR INOX Q4 results: film releases help company rebound to profitability, May 2026

# Vikram Mehra Took Saregama From ₹19 Crore to ₹206 Crore With Songs From the 1950s
URL: https://boardroomcxo.com/article-vikram-mehra-saregama-carvaan
Published: 2026-10-28
Author: CA Ketul Patel, Founder, Boardroom CXO
Publisher: Boardroom CXO (https://boardroomcxo.com)
================================================================================

## Key Takeaways

- In FY14 Saregama's music revenue fell 18.5% to about ₹114 crore. It had licensed its physical music business to Sony DADC in July 2013 and had not bought new film music since the 1990s. Its MD resigned in February 2014.
- Vikram Mehra joined from Tata Sky in October 2014. A 2015 study showed that for listeners over 40, getting to the old songs they loved was a huge hassle. Saregama built Carvaan, a player with 5,000 classic Hindi songs, and it sold a million units in about 16 months.
- In FY26 Saregama's music business brought in ₹684 crore, about six times its FY14 level, and consolidated profit was ₹206 crore against ₹19 crore in FY14. Boards should value what a company already owns before buying something new.

In FY14, Saregama's music revenue fell 18.5%, to about ₹114 crore.

The label, once India's best-known name in film music as HMV, had licensed its physical music business to Sony DADC in July 2013 to focus on digital. It had not bought new film music since the 1990s. In February 2014, its managing director resigned.

On paper, Saregama looked like a company living off its past.

## Who Is Vikram Mehra?

In October 2014, Vikram Mehra joined as managing director. He came from Tata Sky, where he had been chief marketing officer and chief commercial officer, and before that from STAR TV. An IIT Roorkee engineer with an MBA from IIM Lucknow, he had spent his career on marketing, customers and what they actually want.

What he inherited was a catalogue of more than a lakh songs, many of them classics from the 1950s to the 1980s.

## He Started With the Listener, Not the Catalogue

Most leaders in that seat would have chased new film music to look current again. He went back to the people who loved the old songs.

> "In 2015, we conducted a big study about music consumption behaviour in India," he told Outlook Business.

The study, across 23 cities, found something simple: for anybody above 40, getting to the music they loved was a huge hassle. The songs were on phones and apps that this audience did not use easily.

Selling the songs more cheaply was not the answer. Saregama tried that: by 2016 it was offering songs on its website for as little as ₹2 each.

## Carvaan: The Old Songs in a New Box

So Saregama built a product instead. Carvaan, launched in 2017, was a retro-styled music player that came preloaded with 5,000 classic Hindi songs from the 1950s to the 1980s. No app, no download, no internet. Switch it on and the songs play.

It was not cheap. By late 2017 it sold for ₹5,990. It still sold a million units in about 16 months.

The same catalogue was then licensed to the streaming platforms and to video, earning money every time a song was played.

## What the Old Songs Earned

In FY26, Saregama's music business brought in ₹684 crore, about six times its FY14 level. The company's consolidated profit was ₹206 crore, against ₹19 crore in FY14.

Saregama now buys new music again. But the turnaround was built on songs it already owned.

## The Boardroom Lesson: An Old Catalogue Is Not a Dead Asset

When a business is shrinking, boards tend to look outward: new markets, new products, an acquisition. The asset already on the balance sheet, written down and ignored, rarely gets a second look.

> An old catalogue is not a dead asset. It is the one thing no competitor can copy.

Mehra's answer was to find the customers who still wanted the old songs, learn why they were not buying them, and build what they needed.

## Common Mistakes Boards Make With a Legacy Asset

Boards of companies with a large back catalogue, an old brand or a heritage product tend to make the same three errors.

They treat old as worthless. A catalogue that earns little today may be underused, not unwanted. Ask who still values it and what is stopping them from paying.

They compete on price. Selling songs for ₹2 did not change the business. A product built for the customer did, at a premium price.

They chase the newest thing to look current. New film music was where every rival competed. Saregama's edge was the music nobody else owned.

## A Framework for Hiring a Leader to Revive a Legacy Business

When we brief boards on a CXO search for a company with a valuable but underused legacy, we push for three specific checks.
- Look for leaders who start with customer research. Mehra's turn began with a study, not a strategy deck. Ask candidates how they found out what customers actually needed.
- Value marketing and consumer backgrounds for asset-heavy businesses. Saregama's MD came from a pay-TV company, not a music label. Understanding the customer mattered more than knowing the industry.
- Ask what the candidate would do with what the company already owns. The right leader will find value in the existing assets before asking for money to buy new ones.

## Why This Belongs in the Boardroom, Not Just the Business Pages

This sits alongside the story we told of Rajiv Bajaj and the Chetak, another old name that came back on a new product. And it echoes Siddhartha Lal at Royal Enfield, who built growth on a brand others had written off.

The past is not always a burden. In the right hands, it is the asset nobody else has.

## Sources

- MediaNama, Saregama will focus on digital music after licensing physical rights to Sony DADC, July 2013
- MediaNama, Saregama CEO Surya Mantha resigns, February 2014
- MediaNama, Saregama Q4 FY14 earnings, June 2014
- MediaNama, Saregama appoints Tata Sky CCO Vikram Mehra as MD, August 2014
- Techlomedia, Download songs legally from Saregama at just Rs 2 per song, July 2016
- Business Standard (PTI), Carvaan hits one million units sales in 16 months, December 2018
- Outlook Business, Carvaan: A journey begins, March 2019
- Indian Television, Saregama FY26 profit rises as music and artist business strike a chord, May 2026

# Shailesh Chandra Took Over Tata's Cars at Their Low Point. Sales Are Now Nearly 5x.
URL: https://boardroomcxo.com/article-shailesh-chandra-tata-motors
Published: 2026-10-23
Author: CA Ketul Patel, Founder, Boardroom CXO
Publisher: Boardroom CXO (https://boardroomcxo.com)
================================================================================

## Key Takeaways

- Tata Motors sold 5,676 cars in India in March 2020, down 68%, and 1,31,197 in FY20, down 38%, for a market share of about 5%. Shailesh Chandra took charge of the car business on 1 April 2020, as the country locked down.
- He did not chase volume with price cuts. He kept backing electric cars when few Indians bought them and widened the range with the Punch, a small SUV launched in 2021.
- In FY26 Tata sold 6,31,387 cars in India, nearly five times its FY20 volume, including a record 92,120 EVs, and finished the second half as India's No. 2 carmaker by registrations. Boards should judge a turnaround leader on the bets they protect, not the discounts they offer.

In March 2020, Tata Motors sold just 5,676 cars in India, down 68% from a year earlier.

Over the full year FY20, its car sales fell 38%, to 1,31,197, and its share of India's car market was about 5%.

Then the country locked down. Showrooms shut. Factories stopped.

## Who Is Shailesh Chandra?

On 1 April 2020, Shailesh Chandra took charge of Tata Motors' passenger vehicle business.

He was no outsider. He first joined Tata Motors in 1995 as a production manager, spent three years at Tata Sons, and came back in 2016 to run corporate strategy. Before taking over the car business, he had been president of its electric vehicle and corporate strategy work.

Today he is managing director and chief executive of Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles Limited.

## The Two Bets Instead of a Price War

Most leaders in that seat would have cut prices to win buyers back.

He did not. He made two bets instead.

The first was electric cars. Tata kept backing them when very few Indians were buying them, building a range of EVs well before most rivals had one.

The second was the range itself. Tata widened its line-up with the Punch, a small SUV launched in October 2021, that gave first-time SUV buyers a reason to walk into a Tata showroom.

Both bets needed patience. Electric cars, in particular, took years to catch on.

## What the Bets Delivered

In FY26, Tata sold 6,31,387 cars in India, nearly five times its FY20 volume. It sold a record 92,120 electric cars that year. By the second half of FY26, it was India's No. 2 carmaker by Vahan registrations, a position it held into the April to June 2026 quarter.

In electric cars, the lead is wider still. Between April and June 2026, 32,283 of the 82,737 electric cars registered in India were Tatas, about 39%. Demand is now ahead of supply: "In EVs, we are starkly seeing quite a wide gap between demand and supply," Chandra said in July 2026.

Now go back to that worst month of 2020. In March 2026, Tata sold 66,192 cars in India, almost 12 times what it sold six years earlier.

## The Boardroom Lesson: The Low Point Is Where the Next Leader Begins

A collapse in sales invites the quickest fix: discounts, dealer incentives, anything that moves cars this month. It can buy a quarter. It rarely builds a business.

> A brand's lowest point is not its ending. It is where the next leader begins.

Chandra's answer was to protect the long bets, electric cars and a wider SUV range, when the short-term numbers gave every reason to abandon them.

## Common Mistakes Boards Make When a Business Hits Its Low Point

Boards facing a sharp fall in sales tend to make the same three errors.

They buy volume with price. Discounts bring buyers back briefly and train them to wait for the next one. They also eat the money needed for new products.

They cut the long-term bets first. Projects that will not pay for years, like electric cars in 2020, are the easiest to cancel in a crisis. They are often the ones that matter most.

They look outside for a saviour. Chandra had spent most of his career inside Tata Motors. An insider who knows where the long bets are can protect them better than an outsider brought in to cut costs.

## A Framework for Hiring a Leader at a Low Point

When we brief boards on a CXO search for a business at the bottom of a cycle, we push for three specific checks.
- Ask which bets the candidate would protect. The right leader can name the two or three long-term moves that must survive the downturn, and explain why.
- Look for patience backed by numbers. Electric cars took years to pay off. Ask candidates how they kept a board's confidence while a bet was still losing money.
- Consider strong insiders seriously. A leader who has run strategy and new businesses inside the company may already know the way out.

## Why This Belongs in the Boardroom, Not Just the Business Pages

This sits alongside the story we told of Rajiv Bajaj and the Chetak, another leader whose electric bet took years to prove itself. And it is the other side of the story we told of R C Bhargava at Maruti Suzuki, whose market share Tata was among those to take.

The low point is when leaders are most tempted to trade the future for this month's numbers. Boards that hire well find leaders who will not.

## Sources

- Rushlane, Tata Motors March 2020 sales, April 2020
- Rushlane, Mayank Pareek steps down; Shailesh Chandra to head Tata Motors PV business, March 2020
- Storyboard18, Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles March sales rise 29% YoY to 66,971 units, April 2026
- Autocar Professional, Tata EV sales cross 300,000 units, hit a new high in March and FY2026, April 2026
- NSE filing (Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles), Passenger vehicle sales, March 2026 and FY26, April 2026
- Autocar Professional, Q1 FY27: Tata Motors Pulls Clear at No. 2 on Strong Punch, Nexon and Sierra Demand, July 2026
- Autocar Professional, India's Electric-Car Penetration May Touch 8% by FY27-End: Shailesh Chandra, July 2026

# Saugata Gupta Bought Founders, Not D2C Teams. Then He Kept Marico Out.
URL: https://boardroomcxo.com/article-saugata-gupta-marico-d2c
Published: 2026-10-21
Author: CA Ketul Patel, Founder, Boardroom CXO
Publisher: Boardroom CXO (https://boardroomcxo.com)
================================================================================

## Key Takeaways

- Saugata Gupta concluded that a large FMCG company's appetite for risk and failure was wrong for starting digital-first brands, so Marico bought founder-led brands instead: Beardo from 2017, Just Herbs in 2021 and Plix from 2023.
- He kept Marico out of their way. "The moment multiple MBAs start adding value to a brand, these startup brands stutter," he told analysts in January 2021.
- Marico's digital-first brands exited FY26 at an annual run rate above ₹1,100 crore, Plix's revenue doubled to ₹864 crore, and Marico paid over six times more per share of Plix in 2026 than in 2023. Boards should be honest about what their own organisation is built to do.

Saugata Gupta, MD and CEO of Marico, the company behind Parachute and Saffola, has said something few CEOs say out loud: that the company he runs is not built to do everything.

His case in point was digital brands, the kind that are born and sold online.

## Who Is Saugata Gupta?

Saugata Gupta is the managing director and chief executive of Marico. An engineer from IIT Kharagpur and an alumnus of IIM Bangalore, he joined Marico in 2004 and has run it since 2014.

For someone who had spent two decades inside the company, admitting its limits was not a small thing.

## Why He Did Not Build Digital Brands In-House

Gupta's view was that a large FMCG company and a young digital brand need different things. The core business runs on scale and takes few, careful risks. A young D2C brand needs to take many small ones, and to fail often. "The risk-taking appetite is different," he told The Core. After 15 to 20 years in a traditional setup, he said, "it's very difficult to adopt."

Most leaders would have hired a bigger digital team and tried again.

He bought founders instead.

## The Brands He Bought

His first bet came in March 2017. Marico agreed to take a 45% stake in Beardo, a men's grooming brand then well under two years old that made about 75% of its sales online. In 2020 it bought the rest of Beardo. Then came Just Herbs in 2021, and Plix, a plant-based nutrition brand, in July 2023.

Marico usually takes a majority stake, lets the founders keep running the business for a few years, and learns from them before integrating it.

## Keeping Marico Out of the Way

His second decision was harder. He kept the founders independent, even from Marico.

> "One of the reasons startup brands work well is because there is not too much MBA interference. The moment multiple MBAs start adding value to a brand, these startup brands stutter," he told analysts in January 2021.

Beardo ran on its own processes and systems, in a separate business unit for digital brands that operated independently of the rest of Marico.

## What the Founders' Work Is Now Worth

Both decisions paid off. Marico's digital-first brands exited FY26 at an annual revenue run rate of more than ₹1,100 crore. Beardo makes money, and Plix has broken even. Plix's parent company doubled its revenue in FY26, to ₹864 crore from ₹433 crore.

One pair of numbers shows what those founders' work is now worth. In July 2023, Marico agreed to pay ₹369 crore for 58% of Plix, in stages. In October 2026, it paid ₹1,012 crore for another 24.09%, taking its stake to 84%. Per percentage point, that is more than six times the 2023 price, and Marico has agreed to buy the rest by July 2027.

## The Boardroom Lesson: Size Can Fund an Idea, but Rarely Grows One

Large companies have money, distribution and talent. What they often lack is tolerance for the mess that a young brand needs: fast decisions, frequent failures and founders who do not wait for approval.

> Size can fund a new idea. It rarely lets one grow.

Gupta's answer was to separate the two. Marico supplied the capital and the patience. The founders supplied the speed.

## Common Mistakes Boards Make When Buying a Startup Brand

Boards of large consumer companies acquiring D2C and digital-first brands tend to make the same three errors.

They integrate too fast. Moving a young brand onto the parent's systems, processes and approval layers on day one can kill the speed that made it worth buying.

They send in their own managers to fix it. A team trained on large, low-risk brands will often manage a young brand toward caution. Gupta's line about MBAs is the warning.

They judge it on the parent's metrics too early. A brand that is still finding its customers will not look like Parachute in its first years. Give it a path to profit, not the parent's margin on day one.

## A Framework for Hiring Leaders for Digital-First Brands

When we brief boards on a CXO search for a consumer company building or buying digital brands, we push for three specific checks.
- Be honest about what your organisation is built for. If the core business rewards caution, do not expect it to incubate risky brands. Decide early whether to build, buy or partner.
- Hire for entrepreneurial attitude, not just digital experience. Gupta has said Beardo's first CEO came from legacy brands but was an entrepreneur by attitude. That matters more than the CV.
- Protect the founder's room to run. Agree in advance how long founders will run the business, which decisions they keep, and when integration begins.

## Why This Belongs in the Boardroom, Not Just the Business Pages

This sits alongside the story we told of Marico's war with Hindustan Lever: another moment when the company chose a harder, longer path over the obvious one. And it is the other side of the story we told of Varun Alagh at Honasa, a founder who built a digital-first brand into a listed company.

Knowing what your company is not built for is a strategic advantage. Boards that hire well look for leaders who can say it.

## Sources

- Business Standard, Marico buys 45% stake in Zed Lifestyle, March 2017
- Retail4Growth, FMCG major Marico takes over men's grooming startup Beardo, July 2020
- Marico Limited, Q3 FY21 Earnings Conference Call transcript, January 2021
- The Core, Marico CEO Saugata Gupta on its D2C business and India's changing consumption patterns, November 2024
- Business Today, Marico to acquire 58% stake in Satiya Nutraceuticals for Rs 369 crore, July 2023
- Storyboard18, Marico's digital-first brands cross ₹1,100 crore ARR, August 2026
- Kotak Neo, Marico acquires another 24.09% in Plix parent for ₹1,012 crore, raises stake to 84.09%, October 2026


================================================================================
# Sanjiv Puri Let Go of ITC's Hotels. ITC Still Made ₹20,286 Crore.
URL: https://boardroomcxo.com/article-sanjiv-puri-itc-hotels
Published: 2026-10-16
Author: CA Ketul Patel, Founder, Boardroom CXO
Publisher: Boardroom CXO (https://boardroomcxo.com)
================================================================================

## Key Takeaways

- In July 2023 ITC's board approved moving its hotels into a separate company. Over the previous decade they had brought in about 5% of ITC's revenue and profit but taken more than 20% of its capital spending.
- ITC's shares fell about 4% the day the plan was announced, as investors had wanted all of the hotels handed to them. Sanjiv Puri kept 40% anyway, and shareholders approved the plan. The demerger took effect on 1 January 2025.
- In FY26 ITC earned ₹20,286 crore from continuing operations, and ITC Hotels grew profit 29% to ₹821 crore and paid its first dividend. Boards should judge a portfolio decision on what both businesses do afterwards.

In July 2023, Sanjiv Puri, chairman and managing director of ITC Limited, made a choice most leaders avoid.

He let go of the hotels.

## What ITC Was Giving Up

This was no small side business. ITC had run hotels since 1975, and by 2023 it had more than 120 of them across over 70 locations, including some of India's best-known luxury properties.

So why let them go? Two numbers explain it. Over the decade to 2023, the hotels brought in only about 5% of ITC's revenue and profit, yet took more than 20% of the money ITC spent building its businesses. One brokerage said the hotels guzzled capital.

## Who Is Sanjiv Puri?

Sanjiv Puri is the chairman and managing director of ITC. An alumnus of IIT Kanpur and the Wharton School, he has been at ITC since 1986, and became chairman in 2019.

He read the hotel numbers clearly. On 24 July 2023, ITC's board approved, in principle, moving the hotels into a separate company, ITC Hotels.

## The Market Pushed Back

ITC's shares fell about 4% the day the plan was announced, and kept falling the next day. Many investors had wanted all of the hotels handed to them. ITC chose to keep about 40% and give the other 60% directly to its shareholders.

Most leaders would have dropped the plan, or given investors everything they asked for. Puri did neither.

ITC, he said, would stay invested in the hotels business. At the company's annual meeting in August 2023, he argued that the 40% holding would help the new company succeed: it could keep using the ITC name and brands, stabilise its operations and attract other investors to grow faster.

Shareholders backed him. The demerger took effect on 1 January 2025, and the hotels went their own way.

## What Both Sides Did Next

Without the hotels, ITC became a simpler company, built around what Indians buy every day: Aashirvaad atta, Sunfeast biscuits, Bingo! chips, Classmate notebooks.

In FY26, ITC's everyday brands outside cigarettes brought in ₹24,210 crore, up about 10%. Cigarettes, its oldest business, still brought in ₹37,100 crore net of excise, more than any other part of ITC. Together they helped ITC earn a net profit of ₹20,286 crore from continuing operations.

And the hotels did not suffer. ITC Hotels grew its FY26 profit by about 29% to ₹821 crore, then recommended its first-ever dividend. ITC, as its largest shareholder, was one of those who received it.

## The Boardroom Lesson: Knowing When to Let Go

Conglomerates tend to keep businesses because they have always had them. A business with history, prestige and a famous name is the hardest to let go, even when the numbers say it is taking more than it gives.

> Holding on looks like strength. Knowing when to let go is the real one.

Puri's call was not to sell the hotels or shut them. It was to give them their own balance sheet and their own investors, while keeping enough of a stake to help them grow.

## Common Mistakes Boards Make When Separating a Business

Boards weighing a demerger or spin-off tend to make the same three errors.

They keep a business for its prestige. A famous division can still be the wrong use of capital. Look at its share of capital spending next to its share of profit.

They let the first day's share price decide. ITC's shares fell on the announcement. The fair test was what the two businesses did over the following years.

They cut the separated business loose too fast. A clean break pleases some investors, but a new company often needs the parent's brand, people and backing to stand on its own. The size of the retained stake is a strategic choice, not just a financial one.

## A Framework for Leading a Demerger

When we brief boards on a CXO search for a group restructuring its portfolio, we push for three specific checks.
- Find the capital story behind each business. Ask candidates to explain which businesses earn their capital and which consume it. That is where the case for separation starts.
- Look for leaders who can hold a decision under pressure. Investors, analysts and employees will push back. The right leader explains the reasoning and keeps the plan intact.
- Hire a full leadership team for the new company. A demerged business needs its own CEO, CFO and board who can run it as a standalone listed company from day one.

## Why This Belongs in the Boardroom, Not Just the Business Pages

This sits alongside the story we told of Puneet Chhatwal at IHCL, who grew the Taj by owning less of it. Both leaders decided that the best way to grow a hotel business was not to keep putting more of the parent's capital into it.

The hardest portfolio call is the one that gives up something famous. Boards that hire well find leaders who can make it.

## Sources

- Business Today, Why ITC shares fell 4% after hotel demerger news: Jefferies, others explain, July 2023
- Business Standard, ITC hotel demerger financially win-win, says chairman Sanjiv Puri, July 2023
- Business Standard, ITC AGM 2023: Holding in hotels key to success, says chairman Sanjiv Puri, August 2023
- The Week, ITC declines as stock trades post demerger of hotels business, January 2025
- ITC Limited, Quarterly Result Presentation, Q4 FY2026, May 2026
- Free Press Journal, ITC Hotels Q4 Profit Rises 23% To ₹317 Crore, Revenue Climbs To ₹1,254 Crore, May 2026


================================================================================
# Rajiv Bajaj Walked Away From Scooters. Then He Rebuilt the Chetak Name.
URL: https://boardroomcxo.com/article-rajiv-bajaj-chetak
Published: 2026-10-14
Author: CA Ketul Patel, Founder, Boardroom CXO
Publisher: Boardroom CXO (https://boardroomcxo.com)
================================================================================

## Key Takeaways

- In December 2009 Rajiv Bajaj said Bajaj Auto would stop making its last scooter, the Kristal, to focus on motorcycles. His father, chairman Rahul Bajaj, said he was hurt by the decision.
- In October 2019 the Chetak name returned as an electric scooter. Rajiv Bajaj refused to call it a return to scooters: "That would be a wrong inference."
- By 27 June 2026 the electric Chetak had sold 8,00,085 units, and its share of India's electric two-wheeler market rose from 8.3% in 2023 to 22.5% in January to June 2026. Boards should separate what a brand stands for from the product that once carried it.

On 9 December 2009, Rajiv Bajaj told reporters in New Delhi that Bajaj Auto would stop making its last scooter.

The Kristal was selling about 300 units a month. Production would end that financial year. India's most famous scooter maker would make no scooters at all.

## What Was Being Given Up

It is easy to miss how much that meant. The Bajaj Chetak had been in production since 1972. In the licence raj years, when government controls capped how many scooters Bajaj could make, the waiting list was reported to run for years, by some accounts as long as ten. Families planned around a delivery date. "Hamara Bajaj" was not just an advertising line. It described the Indian middle class.

At its peak, Bajaj was the world's largest scooter maker. By 2009, buyers had moved to motorcycles, and the Chetak itself had already been out of production for several years.

## Who Is Rajiv Bajaj?

Rajiv Bajaj is the managing director of Bajaj Auto. He took over as managing director in 2005, the same year Chetak production wound down, and set the company on a single course: to be a motorcycle specialist.

His reasoning on scooters was simple. If Bajaj was to be a motorcycle specialist, he said, it could not make scooters.

## Focus Over Nostalgia

Not everyone agreed. His father, Rahul Bajaj, the chairman who had built the scooter business, said publicly that he was not convinced and that he was hurt by the decision.

Most leaders protect the heirloom. Rajiv Bajaj walked away from scooters altogether, against the wishes of the man who had made them famous.

## The Chetak Comes Back, but Not as a Scooter Comeback

On 16 October 2019, Bajaj Auto unveiled an electric scooter. It carried the Chetak name.

This is where he refused the easy story. The headlines wrote themselves: Hamara Bajaj is back. He declined the lap of honour.

> "Some people think we are changing strategy and are back in scooters. That would be a wrong inference," he told Autocar Professional.

The electric Chetak launched on 14 January 2020 at ₹1 lakh, sold at first through 18 dealerships, 13 in Bengaluru and five in Pune.

It was not the old scooter. It was a new product carrying an old promise.

## What the Name Did Next

By 27 June 2026, the electric Chetak had sold 8,00,085 units, according to Vahan registration data. Its share of India's electric two-wheeler market rose from 8.3% in calendar 2023 to 22.5% in January to June 2026, making Bajaj one of the two largest electric two-wheeler makers in the country.

## The Boardroom Lesson: A Brand Is Not the Product That Once Carried It

A legacy product is easy to defend. It has history, loyal customers and, often, a founder or chairman attached to it. Walking away from it looks like disloyalty.

> A legacy is easy to defend. It is harder to let it go, and then rebuild the name.

Bajaj let go of the product and kept the promise. When the name came back, it came back on something new, built for a different market, and it was judged on what it sold, not on nostalgia.

## Common Mistakes Boards Make With a Legacy Brand

Boards of companies with a famous old product tend to make the same three errors.

They keep the product alive for sentiment. A product selling a few hundred units a month takes management time and capital from the business that is actually growing.

They confuse the brand with the product. What customers remembered about the Chetak was trust and reliability, not two-stroke engines. That is what could be carried into a new product.

They bring the name back as a nostalgia play. A revival sold on memory alone fades fast. The electric Chetak was positioned as a new product, and its numbers had to stand on their own.

## A Framework for Leaders Deciding What to Keep

When we brief boards on a CXO search for a company with a strong legacy brand, we push for three specific checks.
- Ask what the brand actually stands for. The right leader can separate the promise customers trust from the product that currently delivers it.
- Look for leaders who can say no to the founder's favourite. Focus sometimes means ending something the chairman built. Ask candidates when they last stopped a product people loved.
- Hire for the next product, not the last one. Bringing a name back on an electric scooter took engineering, product and marketing leaders who were building for a new market, not restoring an old one.

## Why This Belongs in the Boardroom, Not Just the Business Pages

This sits alongside the story we told of Siddhartha Lal at Royal Enfield, another heir who made hard calls about a famous old two-wheeler brand and was proved right by the sales.

Some legacies are protected by keeping them unchanged. The stronger ones survive being rebuilt.

## Sources

- domain-b, Bajaj announces end of the road for its scooters, December 2009
- Business Standard, Bajaj hurt by son's move to exit scooters, December 2009
- Autocar India, Bajaj Chetak: From inception to rebirth, October 2019
- Autocar Professional, Rajiv Bajaj: 'Some people think we are changing strategy and are back in scooters. That would be a wrong inference.', October 2019
- Autocar India, Bajaj Chetak e-scooter launched at Rs 1 lakh, January 2020
- Autocar India, Bajaj Chetak electric scooter sales cross 8 lakh milestone, June 2026


================================================================================
# Jayen Mehta Took Amul to America Without Exporting a Litre of Milk From India
URL: https://boardroomcxo.com/article-jayen-mehta-amul
Published: 2026-10-09
Author: CA Ketul Patel, Founder, Boardroom CXO
Publisher: Boardroom CXO (https://boardroomcxo.com)
================================================================================

## Key Takeaways

- Amul's brand turnover crossed ₹1 lakh crore in FY26, and GCMMF, the federation that markets it, booked ₹73,450 crore, up 11.4%. It has no share price and no plans for one.
- Amul is owned by about 3.6 million dairy farmers in Gujarat through 18 district cooperative unions. Asked if it would ever list, managing director Jayen Mehta said: buy a cow, become a member of the cooperative.
- Amul entered the US in 2024 with fresh milk collected and processed by the Michigan Milk Producers Association and sold at Costco. Boards should be clear who the business is for before they decide how to grow it.

In FY26, the Amul brand crossed ₹1 lakh crore in turnover, reported as the first Indian FMCG brand to reach that mark.

There was no share price to celebrate it. No IPO. No plans for either.

## Why Amul Will Never List

That is not a funding gap. It is the design.

Amul is owned by about 3.6 million dairy farmers in Gujarat, through 18 district cooperative unions. The Gujarat Cooperative Milk Marketing Federation (GCMMF), which markets the Amul brand, reported its own turnover of ₹73,450 crore in FY26, up 11.4% from ₹65,911 crore. The ₹1 lakh crore figure adds the sales of the district unions on top.

The farmers are not investors waiting for a return on capital. They are the suppliers, and the business exists to pay them as much as it can for their milk.

## Who Is Jayen Mehta?

Jayen Mehta is the managing director of GCMMF. He joined Amul in 1991 from the Institute of Rural Management Anand (IRMA), worked through brand management and marketing roles, and rose to chief operating officer over about 32 years.

He took interim charge as managing director on 9 January 2023, when R S Sodhi stepped down, and was confirmed in the role in December 2024 for a five-year term.

## "Buy a Cow, Become a Member of the Cooperative"

At the Business Today India@100 summit in August 2025, he was asked whether Amul would ever go public. He did not talk about valuation.

> "Buy a cow, become a member of the cooperative," he said.

His point was that a listed company tries to buy cheap and sell high. Amul tries to pay farmers the most it can and give consumers the best value it can, which leaves little room for the kind of profit a stock market would value.

## How Amul Went to America Without Exporting Milk

Most companies at that scale reach for capital markets to grow. Amul reached for American farmers.

On 20 March 2024, at the annual meeting of the Michigan Milk Producers Association (MMPA), a 108-year-old dairy cooperative, Mehta announced that Amul fresh milk would launch in the US. It came in four fat grades, Amul Gold, Shakti, Taaza and Slim, in gallon and half-gallon packs, for the East Coast and Midwest. It was the first time Amul fresh milk had launched outside India.

The part most people miss: none of the milk is shipped from India. MMPA collects and processes it from its own farmer members, and GCMMF brings the brand, the formulations and the marketing.

By October 2024, Amul Gold was on Costco shelves, starting on the East Coast, with a stated plan to reach all of Costco's roughly 750 US stores.

A cooperative from Anand now sells American milk to Americans, and still answers to farmers in Gujarat.

## The Boardroom Lesson: Ownership Decides What a Business Is For

Most growth debates in a boardroom start with capital: how much to raise, at what valuation, from whom. Amul starts somewhere else. Its owners are its suppliers, so every decision is first a question about what it does for them.

> Capital asks what a company is worth. Ownership decides what it is for.

That constraint did not stop Amul growing. It shaped how it grew: through the brand, the distribution and partnerships with other cooperatives, rather than through a share price.

## Common Mistakes Boards Make When Growing an Unlisted Business

Boards of cooperatives, family businesses and other companies without a listing tend to make the same three errors as they scale.

They treat not listing as a weakness. A listing is one way to fund growth. Amul has reached ₹1 lakh crore without it. The question is whether the business can fund its plans, not whether it has a ticker.

They hire leaders who only know the listed playbook. A leader who measures success in valuation will struggle in a business whose owners want higher milk prices, not higher multiples.

They assume going abroad means exporting product. Amul took its brand to the US and left the milk local. Sometimes the asset that travels is the brand and the know-how.

## A Framework for Hiring Leaders Into a Cooperative or Unlisted Business

When we brief boards on a CXO search for a cooperative, family-owned or unlisted company, we push for three specific checks.
- Ask candidates who the business is for. The right leader can say clearly who the owners are and what they want from the business, and will make decisions in that order.
- Look for builders, not financiers. Without a share price to lean on, growth comes from brand, distribution and operations. Hire leaders whose record is built on those.
- Value long tenure and inside knowledge. Mehta spent about 32 years inside Amul before running it. In a business with an unusual ownership model, understanding the system can matter more than outside experience.

## Why This Belongs in the Boardroom, Not Just the Business Pages

This is the next chapter of the story we told of Verghese Kurien, who built the cooperative model that still decides how Amul grows. The leaders have changed. The owners have not.

Before a board decides how to grow, it has to know who the growth is for.

## Sources

- Free Press Journal, Amul Crosses ₹1 Lakh Crore Turnover In FY26, Registers 11% Growth, April 2026
- Dairy Industries International, Amul brand turnover hits one trillion rupees and 11% growth, April 2026
- Business Standard, RS Sodhi steps down as Amul MD; Jayen Mehta given interim charge, January 2023
- Indian Cooperative, Mehta confirmed as MD of GCMMF for five years, December 2024
- Business Today, Jayen Mehta explains why Amul will never launch an IPO (BT India@100), August 2025
- Business Today, A first for India! Amul forays into US market with fresh milk range, March 2024
- DeshGujarat, Amul partners with Costco to launch fresh milk in U.S. retail market, October 2024


================================================================================
# R C Bhargava: Maruti's Share Hit a 13-Year Low. It Still Sold a Record 24 Lakh Cars.
URL: https://boardroomcxo.com/article-rc-bhargava-maruti-suzuki
Published: 2026-10-07
Author: CA Ketul Patel, Founder, Boardroom CXO
Publisher: Boardroom CXO (https://boardroomcxo.com)
================================================================================

## Key Takeaways

- Maruti Suzuki's share of India's passenger vehicle market fell to 39.26% in FY26, a 13-year low and the third straight year of decline, as utility vehicles grew to about two thirds of the market.
- In the same year it sold a record 24.22 lakh vehicles, earned record consolidated revenue of ₹1,83,382 crore, up 19.9%, and exported close to 4.5 lakh vehicles.
- Chairman R C Bhargava, 91, told analysts not to harp on market share and pointed to full capacity, volumes and profit. Boards should be clear which number they are actually running the company on.

Maruti Suzuki, India's largest carmaker, closed FY26 with its share of the passenger vehicle market at 39.26%, according to SIAM data. It was the lowest in thirteen years.

It was not a one-year story.

## Why Maruti's Market Share Fell

FY26 was the third straight year the number had fallen. Maruti had held more than half the market as recently as FY19.

The reason sat inside the industry's own shift. Utility vehicles, SUVs and MPVs, grew to about 67% of India's passenger vehicle sales in FY26. Maruti Suzuki's share inside that segment was below 25%. Every rival gaining ground was gaining it there. Mahindra & Mahindra, for one, more than doubled its overall share in five years, to 14.21%, and became the country's second-largest carmaker.

## Who Is R C Bhargava?

R C Bhargava is the chairman of Maruti Suzuki. A former IAS officer, he joined the company in 1981, when it was a government venture with Suzuki that had yet to build a car, and later served as its managing director. He has been chairman since 2007.

Forty-five years after he joined, at 91, he was still in the chairman's seat when the FY26 number came in.

## What He Said Instead of Defending the Number

When the question came up after the FY26 results in April 2026, he did not defend the market share figure. He questioned why it mattered so much.

> "So please don't harp on market share," he said.

His argument was that a car company should make sure the manufacturing capacity it has installed is fully used, and that it sells those cars at a reasonable profit. Gaining share, he said, would need capacity to be added at a much faster rate. Maruti was already building at two sites at once, at Kharkhoda in Haryana and a new site in Gujarat, and planned capital spending of about ₹14,000 crore for the year.

Most leaders watching share erode reach for a headline SUV launch or a price war. Bhargava pointed to a different set of numbers.

## The Numbers Nobody Asked About

In the year its share hit that 13-year low, Maruti Suzuki sold 24.22 lakh vehicles, its highest ever, up from 22.34 lakh in FY25. Consolidated revenue from operations reached a record ₹1,83,382 crore, up 19.9%. It exported close to 4.5 lakh vehicles, more than any other carmaker in India.

Profit did not keep pace. Consolidated net profit rose only about 1%, to ₹14,680 crore, as costs climbed. The record was in volumes and revenue, not margins.

Its answer on electric cars followed the same logic. Maruti Suzuki's first EV, the e Vitara, was unveiled in January 2025 and launched in India in February 2026, priced from ₹10.99 lakh under a battery subscription plan. Exports began first. By June 2026, nearly 36,000 had been shipped overseas, about five times the roughly 7,000 dispatched to Indian dealers.

Bhargava has not called any of this a comeback.

## The Boardroom Lesson: Market Share Is One Number, Not the Scorecard

Market share is the number analysts and the press quote back at a company. It is easy to read and easy to compare. But it is a ratio, and a ratio can fall while everything underneath it grows.

> A shrinking share can still sit on top of a record year. The two numbers were never really arguing with each other.

The harder question for a board is not whether share is falling. It is whether the company is losing the customers it actually wants, at the margins it needs, in the segments that will matter in five years.

## Common Mistakes Boards Make When Market Share Falls

Boards of market leaders in autos, consumer goods and other scale businesses tend to make the same three errors when share starts to slip.

They treat share as the only scorecard. A leader can lose share while selling more, earning more and exporting more. Judge the business on volume, revenue and profit alongside share, not instead of them.

They buy share back with price. A price war wins headlines and costs margin. Maruti's flat profit in a record revenue year shows how little room there is for that.

They ignore where the share is going. Maruti's share loss sat almost entirely in utility vehicles. A board that only watches the headline number misses which segment, and which customers, it is actually losing.

## A Framework for Judging a Leader When Share Falls

When we brief boards on a CXO search for a market leader under pressure, we push for three specific checks.
- Split the share number by segment. Find out where the share is going. A fall concentrated in one fast-growing segment needs a product answer, not a sales push.
- Look at capacity, volume and profit together. If the plants are full and volumes are at a record, the constraint may be capacity, not demand. Ask leadership candidates which number they would manage to, and why.
- Hire for the segment you are losing. Winning back utility vehicle buyers takes product, marketing and sales leaders who have built in that segment, not just leaders from the segment the company already dominates.

## Why This Belongs in the Boardroom, Not Just the Business Pages

This sits alongside the story we told of Gopal Vittal at Airtel, who let millions of low-paying customers go and was judged on revenue per user, not subscriber count. And it is the other side of the story we told of Anish Shah at Mahindra, one of the rivals that gained the share Maruti lost.

The share number will always be the first one quoted. Boards that hire well ask what sits underneath it.

## Sources

- Outlook Business, Maruti Suzuki Loses Market Grip Amid SUV Shift, Share Slips to 13-year Low in FY26, April 2026
- Autocar Professional, SUV, MPV Sales Cross 3 Million for the First Time in FY2026, UV Share of PVs Jumps to 67%, April 2026
- Autocar Professional, "Don't Harp on Market Share": Maruti Suzuki's RC Bhargava Amid Aggressive Scale-up Plans, April 2026
- Autocar Professional, Maruti Suzuki Posts Record FY26 Revenue, but Profit Stays Flat As Costs Climb, April 2026
- Free Press Journal, Maruti Suzuki crosses 24,22,713 units in FY26 with record domestic and export volumes, April 2026
- electrive, India: Maruti Suzuki launches the e-Vitara as its first EV, February 2026
- Autocar Professional, Maruti e-Vitara Sales in India Cross 7,000 Units, Exports Exceed 35,000 Units, June 2026


================================================================================
# Ashok Vaswani: The RBI Banned Kotak on His 115th Day. He Had It Lifted.
URL: https://boardroomcxo.com/article-ashok-vaswani-kotak-mahindra-bank
Published: 2026-10-02
Author: CA Ketul Patel, Founder, Boardroom CXO
Publisher: Boardroom CXO (https://boardroomcxo.com)
================================================================================

## Key Takeaways

- On 24 April 2024, Ashok Vaswani's 115th day as CEO, the RBI barred Kotak Mahindra Bank from onboarding customers online and issuing new credit cards, over IT failures its examinations had found in 2022 and 2023.
- The shares fell up to 13% the next day, nearly ₹40,000 crore of market value went, and Axis Bank overtook Kotak as India's fourth most valuable bank. Vaswani did not blame his predecessors; he worked on the fix with the regulator.
- The RBI lifted the curbs on 12 February 2025, day 409. Boards should judge a leader who inherits a regulatory problem on how fast and how quietly it gets fixed, not on who caused it.

On 24 April 2024, the Reserve Bank of India ordered Kotak Mahindra Bank to stop onboarding new customers through its online and mobile channels and to stop issuing new credit cards, with immediate effect.

It was Ashok Vaswani's 115th day as the bank's chief executive.

## Who Is Ashok Vaswani?

Ashok Vaswani is the managing director and chief executive of Kotak Mahindra Bank. He took over on 1 January 2024 from Uday Kotak, who founded the bank and ran it for nearly four decades. Vaswani was brought in from outside, after a career that included senior leadership roles at Citi and Barclays.

He had less than four months in the job before the regulator acted.

## What the RBI Did, and Why

The RBI acted under Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act. It cited serious concerns from its IT examinations of the bank for 2022 and 2023, covering areas such as IT risk management and information security, which it said the bank had not fixed. A major outage of the bank's core banking and digital channels on 15 April 2024 came just before the order.

Existing customers, including credit card holders, could keep using their accounts. But for a bank that had built much of its recent growth on digital onboarding, the order cut off the main way it added new customers.

The market's answer came the next morning. Kotak's shares fell up to 13% on 25 April, nearly ₹40,000 crore of market value went in a day, and Axis Bank overtook Kotak as India's fourth most valuable bank.

## What He Did Instead of Explaining Whose Fault It Was

The failures the RBI cited came from examinations of 2022 and 2023, before Vaswani joined. He had the easiest defence available to any new chief executive: this happened before me.

He did not use it. In a letter to customers the next day, he wrote that the bank was "actively working to address the concerns raised" and was in constant communication with the regulator.

Then the bank did the slow, unglamorous work. It rebuilt the IT systems and controls the RBI had flagged, and an external audit, commissioned with the RBI's prior approval, checked that the fixes held. Branches kept opening accounts while the digital doors stayed shut.

On 12 February 2025, satisfied with the bank's submissions, the remedial measures and the audit, the RBI lifted the curbs. It was day 409 of Vaswani's tenure.

The results followed. For the January to March 2026 quarter, Kotak reported a standalone net profit of ₹4,027 crore, up 13.4% from a year earlier, as provisions fell sharply.

In June 2026, Vaswani announced that he would not seek reappointment when his term ends on 31 December 2026, citing personal reasons. The bank has begun the search for his successor.

## The Boardroom Lesson: You Inherit the Problem the Day You Take the Job

A new leader's first instinct is to draw a line between the old regime and the new one. Sometimes that line matters. But a regulator does not care which chief executive caused the problem. It cares who fixes it, and how fast.

> A regulator's ban is a verdict on the past. What a bank does next is the only verdict that counts.

Vaswani treated the ban as his problem from the first day, and the fix as his job. That is why the story ends on day 409, not on day 115.

## Common Mistakes Boards Make When a New CEO Inherits a Regulatory Problem

Boards of banks, NBFCs and other regulated businesses tend to make the same three errors when the regulator acts early in a new leader's tenure.

They let the new leader blame the past in public. It may be accurate, but it tells the regulator and the market that the bank is still arguing about the problem instead of fixing it.

They judge the leader on the share price in the first month. The fall on day 116 was about the order, not about the new chief executive. The fair measure is how long it takes to get the order lifted.

They treat technology and compliance as someone else's department. The RBI's concerns were about IT risk and information security. In a modern bank, those sit at the top table, and so do the people who run them.

## A Framework for Hiring a Leader Into a Regulated Business

When we brief boards on a CXO search for a bank, NBFC, insurer or fintech, we push for three specific checks.
- Ask how the candidate handled an inherited problem. Look for leaders who owned what they walked into and fixed it, not ones whose story is mainly about what the last team got wrong.
- Check their record with regulators. The best leaders in regulated businesses keep the regulator informed before it has to ask. Ask referees how the candidate behaved when the regulator was unhappy.
- Hire technology and risk leaders at the same level as the business heads. Kotak's curbs were an IT governance problem. The CTO, CISO and chief risk officer need the standing to stop growth when the systems cannot carry it.

## Why This Belongs in the Boardroom, Not Just the Business Pages

This sits alongside the story we told of Suresh Narayanan at Nestlé India: another leader who walked into a regulator's ban he had not caused, and was judged on how he got the business back, not on how it got there.

A ban tells you what went wrong before. The leader's answer tells you what happens next.

## Sources

- Business Today, Kotak Mahindra Bank shares in focus as RBI bars onboarding new customers online, fresh credit cards, April 2024
- ThePrint (PTI), Kotak Mahindra Bank shares tank nearly 12 pc; mcap erodes by Rs 39,768 cr post RBI action, April 2024
- Business Today, Axis Bank pips Kotak Mahindra Bank to become 4th most-valued bank, April 2024
- NDTV Profit, Kotak Mahindra Bank Chief Reassures Customers After RBI Whip On Key Services, April 2024
- Business Standard, RBI lifts restrictions on Kotak Mahindra Bank on onboarding new customers, February 2025
- Business Today, Kotak Mahindra Bank Q4 results: dividend announced, check earnings summary, May 2026
- Business Today, Kotak Mahindra Bank CEO Ashok Vaswani to step down in December; board begins succession hunt, June 2026


================================================================================
# Falguni Nayar: Nykaa's Stock Fell, Its Profit Grew Nearly Tenfold
URL: https://boardroomcxo.com/article-falguni-nayar-nykaa
Published: 2026-09-30
Author: CA Ketul Patel, Founder, Boardroom CXO
Publisher: Boardroom CXO (https://boardroomcxo.com)
================================================================================

## Key Takeaways

- Nykaa listed on 10 November 2021 at 79% above its issue price and crossed ₹1 lakh crore in market value on its first day.
- Within a year the stock fell 24% in a month and dropped out of India's 100 most valuable companies, but Falguni Nayar kept growing revenue by a quarter or more a year.
- Profit rose from ₹21 crore in FY23 to ₹204 crore in FY26 on revenue of ₹10,022 crore. Boards should judge a founder on the profit line, not the share price.

On 10 November 2021, Nykaa, the beauty and fashion e-commerce company founded by Falguni Nayar, listed on the NSE at 79% above its issue price and crossed ₹1 lakh crore in market value on its first day.

Not everyone bought the celebration.

## Who Is Falguni Nayar?

Falguni Nayar is the founder, executive chairperson, managing director and chief executive of FSN E-Commerce Ventures, the company behind Nykaa. She spent about 25 years in finance and was managing director of Kotak Mahindra Capital when she left to start Nykaa in 2012, at 49, in a country where organised beauty retail barely existed.

> "I was not afraid to be different," she told Fortune in early 2022.

Within months, the market gave her something new to be different about.

## What Happened to the Stock

The euphoria did not last a year. In October 2022, ahead of the end of the one-year lock-in for pre-IPO investors, the stock fell 24% in a single month, dropped close to its ₹1,125 issue price and fell out of India's 100 most valuable companies. It was down more than half from its November 2021 high.

The commentary turned cruel: another glamour D2C listing that could not survive contact with the real market.

## What She Did Instead of Explaining the Share Price

Most founders in that position start explaining the share price. She did not.

She kept doing what the business had been doing quietly since its IPO: growing revenue by a quarter or more every year, while the market told a different story. Revenue rose 36% in FY23, and kept growing in the mid-twenties after that.

Then the numbers closed the gap. Nykaa's net profit rose from ₹21 crore in FY23 to ₹72 crore in FY25 and ₹204 crore in FY26. Revenue crossed ₹10,000 crore for the first time, at ₹10,022 crore, making FY26 the company's first year above $1 billion in revenue. EBITDA grew 59% to ₹752 crore, and its fashion business turned EBITDA-positive.

In November 2025, with that turnaround on the books, Nykaa's board reappointed Falguni Nayar as executive chairperson, managing director and CEO for another five years, from February 2026.

## The Boardroom Lesson: Sentiment and Business Are Two Different Verdicts

Most coverage of a falling stock treats the share price as the scorecard. It is one scorecard, and it moves on lock-in dates, sector moods and the last big listing that disappointed. The other scorecard is slower: revenue, margin and profit, quarter after quarter.

> A falling stock is a verdict on sentiment. A rising profit line is a verdict on the business.

Nayar's answer to the first verdict was to keep working on the second. It took about three and a half years for the profit line to make the point for her.

## Common Mistakes Boards Make When a Founder's Stock Falls After a Hot Listing

Boards of newly listed consumer and internet companies, and the investors watching them, tend to make the same three errors.

They treat the listing-day price as the baseline. A debut 79% above the issue price sets an expectation the business did not set. Judging the leader against that number punishes them for the market's excitement, not their own results.

They read lock-in selling as a verdict on the company. Nykaa's sharpest fall came as early investors were about to be free to sell. That says something about supply of shares. It says little about whether customers were still buying.

They push the founder to chase the share price. The easy response to a falling stock is a new story for investors. The harder one is to keep building the business the stock was supposed to be about.

## A Framework for Evaluating a Founder-CEO After a Post-IPO Fall

When we brief boards on a CXO search for a newly listed consumer, beauty or D2C company, we push for three specific checks.
- Look at revenue growth through the bad stretch. If revenue kept growing by a quarter or more a year while the stock fell, the problem was the price, not the business.
- Track the profit line, not the headline. Nykaa's profit went from ₹21 crore to ₹204 crore over three years. Ask leadership candidates which line they would be judged on, and how long they would need.
- Check that the team can carry the next stage. Getting a business past ₹10,000 crore of revenue needs leaders across marketing, category, supply chain and finance who can keep growth and margin moving together.

## Why This Belongs in the Boardroom, Not Just the Business Pages

This sits alongside the story we told of Varun Alagh at Honasa: another beauty company that listed to big expectations, lost the market's confidence, and won it back with results rather than statements.

The share price will always deliver its verdict first. Boards that hire well wait for the second one.

# Varun Alagh: When Honasa Fell 40%, He Bought More
URL: https://boardroomcxo.com/article-varun-alagh-honasa-mamaearth
Published: 2026-09-25
Author: CA Ketul Patel, Founder, Boardroom CXO
Publisher: Boardroom CXO (https://boardroomcxo.com)
================================================================================

## Key Takeaways

- Honasa Consumer, Mamaearth's parent, posted its first quarterly loss as a listed company in November 2024 and its stock fell about 40% to around ₹223.
- Co-founder and CEO Varun Alagh bought shares twice: about ₹4.5 crore in December 2024 and ₹50 crore in December 2025, taking the promoter group above 35%.
- Quarterly profit reached ₹39 crore and then ₹50 crore, and by September 2026 the stock was near ₹480. Boards should ask whether a founder's conviction comes with a fix, not just a signal.

It started with a question, not a business plan. In 2016, Ghazal Alagh's infant son developed a skin reaction, and when the family went looking for a genuinely toxin-free baby product in India, they could not find one. So they built one.

Mamaearth launched with six baby-care products, and the question behind all of them was simple: is this safe for my child?

Eight years later, that question had grown into Honasa Consumer, which calls itself India's largest digital-first beauty and personal care company. Then, in November 2024, the market decided the story was over.

## Who Is Varun Alagh?

Varun Alagh is the co-founder and chief executive of Honasa Consumer, the house of brands behind Mamaearth. He founded the company with his wife, Ghazal Alagh, in 2016, and took it public in November 2023 at ₹324 a share.

## What Happened in November 2024

For the quarter to September 2024, Honasa reported a net loss of about ₹19 crore, against a profit of ₹29 crore a year earlier. It was the company's first quarterly loss since listing. Revenue fell about 7%.

The cause had a name. Project Neev, a change to how Honasa sold through distributors in India's 50 largest cities, removed a layer from its distribution network and forced a ₹63 crore correction of the inventory sitting with stockists.

The stock hit its 20% lower circuit on 18 November, below its own IPO price, and kept falling. About ₹3,500 crore of market value was erased in two trading sessions. By the end of that week the shares had fallen as much as 40%, to a low of about ₹223. Commentators started writing the obituary early: another overhyped D2C listing, unravelling on schedule.

## What He Did Instead of Arguing

Varun Alagh did not put out a statement disputing that story. He bought the stock instead. A filing in early December 2024 showed he had spent about ₹4.5 crore of his own money on Honasa shares, taking his stake to 31.93%. The stock hit its upper circuit the day the news came out.

That would have been the easy place to stop. He did not. The quarters began to turn: for the three months to September 2025, Honasa reported a profit of ₹39 crore against a loss a year before. Then, on 29 December 2025, with the company still proving itself one quarter at a time, he bought again. About 18.5 lakh shares this time, at ₹270 each, roughly ₹50 crore, from early investor Fireside Ventures. That took his own stake to 32.45% and the promoter group's holding above 35%.

The next quarter, profit reached ₹50 crore, up 93% on the year before, on revenue up 16% to about ₹602 crore. Mamaearth itself was growing again.

> "Our flagship brand is back to double digit growth, driven by product superiority," Mr. Alagh said.

The stock that once traded at ₹223 was near ₹480 by September 2026.

## The Boardroom Lesson: Markets Test Conviction With Numbers

Most coverage of a crashing stock asks what management will say. Alagh's answer was not a statement. It was a filing showing more of his own money in the company, and then a second, much larger one a year later.

> A market tests conviction with numbers. Founders answer it with their own money.

Buying shares is a signal, not a fix. What made it credible was that the fix was already under way: the distribution change that caused the loss was the same change the company kept working through, and the profit that followed came from the business, not from the share price.

## Common Mistakes Boards Make When a Founder-Led Company Hits Its First Bad Quarter

Boards of listed D2C and consumer companies, and the investors watching them, tend to make the same three errors.

They read one bad quarter as the end of the story. Honasa's loss came from a deliberate distribution change with a known, one-time inventory cost. That is a different problem from demand disappearing, and it deserves a different response.

They mistake a founder's share purchase for a plan. Insider buying tells you what the founder believes. It does not tell you whether the operating fix will work. Boards should ask for both, and judge them separately.

They rush to replace leadership before the fix has had time to work. Honasa's recovery took four quarters to show. A board that changed the CEO in the first one would have reset the clock on a change that was already paying back.

## A Framework for Evaluating a Founder-CEO After a Stock Crash

When we brief boards on a CXO search for a founder-led consumer or D2C brand going through a rough stretch, we push for three specific checks.
- Separate the cause from the reaction. Ask what actually caused the bad quarter. A one-time cost from a deliberate change, like Project Neev's inventory correction, calls for patience. A loss of customers calls for a different conversation.
- Look at what the founder does with their own money. Alagh bought twice, a year apart, the second time more than ten times larger. Repeated buying while results are still uncertain says more than a single purchase timed to a press cycle.
- Hire the leaders who make the fix stick. A founder's conviction does not run a distribution network. The quarters turned because sales, supply chain and brand teams executed the change. Ask whether the team around the founder can carry it.

## Why This Belongs in the Boardroom, Not Just the Business Pages

This sits alongside the story we told of Sudhir Sitapati at Godrej Consumer: a consumer business where the leader's choices only made sense once enough quarters had passed to judge them. Honasa's version played out in public, on a stock price that fell faster than the business did.

The market will always test a founder with numbers. The founders worth backing answer with a plan, and with their own money behind it.

- Business Standard, Honasa Consumer stock tanks 20%, hits 52-week low on weak Q2 results, November 2024

- Inc42, Honasa Q3: Profit Zooms 93% YoY To ₹50 Cr, February 2026
